claims.source: Conditional knockout of Epac2 from midbrain dopamine neurons (Epac2-cKO) and the selective Epac2 inhibitor ESI-05 decreased cocaine self-administration in mice under both fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules and across a broad range of cocaine doses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2A-G showing reduced cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice.

claims.claim: The selective Epac2 inhibitor ESI-05 decreased cocaine self-administration in mice under both fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules.
claims.source: Conditional knockout of Epac2 from midbrain dopamine neurons (Epac2-cKO) and the selective Epac2 inhibitor ESI-05 decreased cocaine self-administration in mice under both fixed-ratio and progressive-ratio reinforcement schedules and across a broad range of cocaine doses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1B-H showing dose-dependent reduction in cocaine self-administration with ESI-05 treatment.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO led to reduced evoked dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
claims.source: In addition, Epac2-cKO led to reduced evoked dopamine release, whereas Epac2 agonism robustly enhanced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4 showing decreased dopamine release in Epac2-cKO mice.

claims.claim: Epac2 agonism robustly enhanced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
claims.source: In addition, Epac2-cKO led to reduced evoked dopamine release, whereas Epac2 agonism robustly enhanced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in vitro.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5 showing increased dopamine release with S-220 (Epac2 agonist) treatment.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of VTA dopamine neurons via DCZ-induced activation of Gs-DREADD increased dopamine release and reversed the impairment of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.source: This mechanism is central to the behavioral effects of Epac2 disruption, as chemogenetic stimulation of ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine neurons via deschloroclozapine (DCZ)-induced activation of Gs-DREADD increased dopamine release and reversed the impairment of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6 showing restoration of cocaine self-administration with rM3D(Gs) activation.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons with Gi-DREADD reduced dopamine release and cocaine self-administration in wild-type mice.
claims.source: Conversely, chemogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons with Gi-DREADD reduced dopamine release and cocaine self-administration in wild-type mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7 showing reduced cocaine self-administration with hM4D(Gi) activation.

claims.claim: The rewarding effects of cocaine are primarily mediated by enhanced dopaminergic transmission in the mesolimbic dopamine system.
claims.source: The rewarding effects of cocaine are primarily mediated by enhanced dopaminergic transmission in the mesolimbic dopamine system (Anderson and Pierce, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson and Pierce, 2005.

claims.claim: Repeated cocaine exposure induces an upregulation of cAMP signaling in the VTA and NAc.
claims.source: Repeated cocaine exposure induces an upregulation of cAMP signaling in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and nucleus accumbens (NAc) (Nestler, 2001; Self, 2004; Nestler, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nestler, 2001; Self, 2004; Nestler, 2016.

claims.claim: Repeated cocaine exposure decreases Gαi/o expression in the VTA, which results in elevated cAMP levels.
claims.source: In the VTA, repeated cocaine exposure has been shown to decrease Gαi/o expression (Nestler et al., 1990; Striplin and Kalivas, 1992), which results in elevated cAMP levels.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nestler et al., 1990; Striplin and Kalivas, 1992.

claims.claim: PKA and Epac are two major intracellular cAMP effectors.
claims.source: Protein kinase A (PKA) and exchange protein directly activated by cAMP (Epac) are two major intracellular cAMP effectors (de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012) and have numerous downstream signaling targets, thereby transducing changes in cAMP levels to cellular adaptations that can promote behavioral changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012.

claims.claim: Epac2 is predominately expressed in the brain, whereas Epac1 expression in the brain is very low.
claims.source: Epac2 is predominately expressed in the brain, whereas Epac1 expression in the brain is very low (de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Rooij et al., 1998; Kawasaki et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Epac2, but not Epac1, regulates adaptations in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity in VTA dopamine neurons induced by non-contingent cocaine exposure.
claims.source: By making whole-cell recordings in ex vivo slices prepared from Epac1 and Epac2 global knockout mice (Yang et al., 2012), we have shown that Epac2, but not Epac1, regulates adaptations in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity in VTA dopamine neurons induced by non-contingent cocaine exposure (Liu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Liu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2017) and Yang et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Epac activators enhance presynaptic glutamate release by increasing the association between the active zone proteins Rab3A, RIM and Munc13, thereby facilitating vesicle docking and exocytosis.
claims.source: Epac activators enhance presynaptic glutamate release by increasing the association between the active zone proteins Rab3A, RIM and Munc13, thereby facilitating vesicle docking and exocytosis (Ozaki et al., 2000; Ferrero et al., 2013; Fernandes et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ozaki et al., 2000; Ferrero et al., 2013; Fernandes et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Axonal dopamine release in the striatum is mediated by vesicular exocytosis and requires active zone-like site machinery.
claims.source: Axonal dopamine release in the striatum is mediated by vesicular exocytosis and requires active zone-like site machinery (Liu and Kaeser, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu and Kaeser, 2019.

claims.claim: Dopamine neuron-specific knockout of RIM abolished action potential-triggered dopamine release in the striatum.
claims.source: Dopamine neuron-specific knockout of RIM abolished action potential-triggered dopamine release in the striatum (Liu et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2018a.

claims.claim: The average number of sessions to reach stable acquisition of cocaine self-administration was 5.4±0.3 sessions.
claims.source: The average number of sessions to reach stable acquisition was 5.4±0.3 sessions (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A showing training sessions.

claims.claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes during cocaine self-administration.
claims.source: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes (Figure 1B) and cocaine infusions (Figure 1C) but had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes (Figure 1D; detailed statistics for this and subsequent results are described in the figure legends).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B showing dose-dependent reduction in active nose pokes with ESI-05 treatment.

claims.claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced cocaine infusions during self-administration.
claims.source: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes (Figure 1B) and cocaine infusions (Figure 1C) but had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes (Figure 1D; detailed statistics for this and subsequent results are described in the figure legends).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C showing dose-dependent reduction in cocaine infusions with ESI-05 treatment.

claims.claim: ESI-05 had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes during cocaine self-administration.
claims.source: ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced active nose pokes (Figure 1B) and cocaine infusions (Figure 1C) but had no significant effect on inactive nose pokes (Figure 1D; detailed statistics for this and subsequent results are described in the figure legends).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D showing no significant effect on inactive nose pokes.

claims.claim: No significant sex differences were observed for cocaine self-administration measures.
claims.source: Consistent with a previous study (Slosky et al., 2021), no significant sex differences were observed for any measure, thus the data were pooled across sexes in subsequent studies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data and a citation to Slosky et al., 2021.

claims.claim: ESI-05 pretreatments produced a significant downward shift in the dose-response curve for cocaine infusions.
claims.source: ESI-05 pretreatments produced a significant downward shift in the dose-response curve for cocaine infusions (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA: ESI-05 treatment, F2,22 = 45.5, p<0.001; cocaine dose, F6,132 = 51.0, p<0.001; ESI-05 treatment × cocaine dose interaction, F12,132 = 6.5, p<0.001; 3.3 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05, red *; 10 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05, violet *; 3.3 vs. 10 mg/kg ESI-05 black #) and decreased total cocaine intake (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA: ESI-05 treatment, F2,22 = 66.5, p<0.001; cocaine dose, F6,132 = 498.1, p<0.001; ESI-05 × cocaine dose interaction, F12,132 = 6.7, p<0.001; 3.3 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05, red *; 10 vs. 0 mg/kg ESI-05 violet *; 3.3 vs. 10 mg/kg ESI-05 black #) on the dose-response curve (n=8–9, 5 male and 4 female).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1E-F.

claims.claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased the number of cocaine infusions under a PR reinforcement schedule.
claims.source: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased the number of cocaine infusions (one-way ANOVA: F2,28 = 16.1, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) and breakpoint (Brown-Forsythe equal variance: p<0.05; Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA on ranks: ESI-05, H=17.5, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) under a PR reinforcement schedule.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1G-H.

claims.claim: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased breakpoint under a PR reinforcement schedule.
claims.source: ESI-05 dose-dependently decreased the number of cocaine infusions (one-way ANOVA: F2,28 = 16.1, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) and breakpoint (Brown-Forsythe equal variance: p<0.05; Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA on ranks: ESI-05, H=17.5, p<0.001; n=10–11, 5 male and 5–6 female) under a PR reinforcement schedule.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1G-H.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO mice and WT controls were grossly normal in terms of survival, physical appearance, body weight, and baseline locomotor activity.
claims.source: Epac2-cKO mice (Slc6a3IREScre/+/Epac2loxP/loxP) and WT controls (Slc6a3IREScre/+/Epac2wt/wt or Slc6a3+/+/Epac2loxP/loxP) were grossly normal in terms of survival, physical appearance, body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and baseline locomotor activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Epac2 was expressed in both Th+ and Gad2+ neurons in the VTA of WT mice.
claims.source: We found that Epac2 was expressed in both Th+ and Gad2+ neurons in the VTA of WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but was only detected in Gad2+ neurons and not in Th+ neurons in the VTA of Epac2-cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Epac2 was only detected in Gad2+ neurons and not in Th+ neurons in the VTA of Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.source: We found that Epac2 was expressed in both Th+ and Gad2+ neurons in the VTA of WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but was only detected in Gad2+ neurons and not in Th+ neurons in the VTA of Epac2-cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Epac1 was rarely expressed in neurons of WT and Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.source: Epac1 was rarely expressed in neurons of WT and Epac2-cKO mice, consistent with low expression of Epac1 in the brain (Kawasaki et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data and a citation to Kawasaki et al., 1998.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in the frequency of action potential firing or membrane capacitance in VTA dopamine neurons between WT and Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.source: We also compared the electrophysiological properties of VTA dopamine neurons from WT and Epac2-cKO mice and found no significance differences in the frequency of action potential firing or membrane capacitance (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference between the percentage of WT and Epac2-cKO mice that acquired stable cocaine self-administration after 10 sessions.
claims.source: There was no significant difference between the percentage of mice in each genotype that acquired stable cocaine self-administration after 10 sessions, with 90.9% (10 of 11) of WT and 84.6% (11 of 13) of Epac2-cKO mice with patent catheters meeting the criteria for stable self-administration (χ2=0.024, p=0.877).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of acquisition rates.

claims.claim: The average number of training sessions to reach criteria for stable self-administration was not significantly different between WT and Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.source: Of the mice that acquired stable self-administration, the average number of training sessions to reach criteria was not significantly different between genotypes (WT, 5.4±0.5 sessions; Epac2-cKO, 6.8±0.7 sessions; t19=1.6, p=0.130).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of training sessions.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in active nose pokes during cocaine self-administration training.
claims.source: However, Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in active nose pokes (Figure 2A) and cocaine infusions (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in cocaine infusions during self-administration training.
claims.source: However, Epac2-cKO mice showed significant decreases in active nose pokes (Figure 2A) and cocaine infusions (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Inactive nose pokes were not significantly different between WT and Epac2-cKO mice during cocaine self-administration.
claims.source: Inactive nose pokes were not significantly different between genotypes (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO mice exhibited a downward shift in the cocaine dose-response curve.
claims.source: Epac2-cKO mice displayed a significant downward shift in the cocaine dose-response curve compared with WT mice (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO mice exhibited lower cocaine intake than WT mice across multiple cocaine doses.
claims.source: Epac2-cKO mice also exhibited lower cocaine intake than WT mice (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO mice acquired significantly fewer cocaine infusions under a PR reinforcement schedule.
claims.source: Epac2-cKO mice acquired significantly fewer cocaine infusions (Figure 2F) and had a significantly reduced breakpoint (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO mice had a significantly reduced breakpoint under a PR reinforcement schedule.
claims.source: Epac2-cKO mice acquired significantly fewer cocaine infusions (Figure 2F) and had a significantly reduced breakpoint (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: ESI-05 had no significant effect on active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or sucrose intake under an FR1 reinforcement schedule.
claims.source: ESI-05 had no significant effect on active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or sucrose intake (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: ESI-05 did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint under a PR reinforcement schedule.
claims.source: Again, ESI-05 did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F) under this reinforcement schedule.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO did not affect the acquisition of sucrose self-administration under an FR1 schedule.
claims.source: Under an FR1 schedule, there was no significant effect of genotype on active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or sucrose intake across the 10-day session (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A-C.

claims.claim: Epac2-cKO did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint under a PR schedule.
claims.source: Similarly, Epac2-cKO did not affect sucrose intake or breakpoint under a PR schedule (Figure 3D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to single pulse stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice.
claims.source: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to single pulse and high-frequency burst stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions sampled in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 4A, B, D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to high-frequency burst stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice.
claims.source: The peak amplitudes of evoked dopamine release in response to single pulse and high-frequency burst stimulation were significantly decreased across all striatum subregions sampled in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 4A, B, D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4D-E.

claims.claim: There were no significant changes in the exponential decay constant τ of evoked dopamine responses from either single pulse or high-frequency burst stimulation across all striatum subregions in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice.
claims.source: We found that there were no significant changes in τ from either single pulse or high-frequency burst stimulation across all striatum subregions sampled in slices from Epac2-cKO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 4A, C, D and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 4C and F.

claims.claim: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices.
claims.source: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices (Figure 5A–B), which was blocked by Epac2-cKO (Figure 5C) and ESI-05 (20 µM, Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5A-B.

claims.claim: The S-220-induced increase in evoked dopamine release was blocked by Epac2-cKO.
claims.source: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices (Figure 5A–B), which was blocked by Epac2-cKO (Figure 5C) and ESI-05 (20 µM, Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The S-220-induced increase in evoked dopamine release was blocked by ESI-05.
claims.source: Bath application of S-220 led to a concentration-dependent increase in evoked dopamine release in WT slices (Figure 5A–B), which was blocked by Epac2-cKO (Figure 5C) and ESI-05 (20 µM, Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The PKA inhibitor H89 had no effect on the S-220-induced increase in dopamine release.
claims.source: In contrast, the PKA inhibitor H89 (1 μM) had no effect (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Bath application of 6-Bnz-cAMP increased dopamine release in the NAc shell in slices from WT mice.
claims.source: Bath application of 6-Bnz-cAMP (1 µM) increased dopamine release in the NAc shell in slices from WT mice (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The 6-Bnz-cAMP-induced increase in dopamine release was blocked by H89.
claims.source: This effect was blocked by H89 but was not altered by Epac-cKO (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The 6-Bnz-cAMP-induced increase in dopamine release was not altered by Epac2-cKO.
claims.source: This effect was blocked by H89 but was not altered by Epac-cKO (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FSCV data presented in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: rM3D(Gs) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA.
claims.source: rM3D(Gs) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons (85.3 ± 4.2% and 87.1 ± 5.3%, respectively) but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: DCZ significantly increased the frequency of dopamine transients in the NAc shell of Epac2-cKO mice following vehicle pretreatment.
claims.source: Subcutaneous injection of DCZ (100 µg/kg) 20 min after i.p. vehicle pretreatment caused a rapid and robust increase (~30 min) in the frequency of dopamine transients in the NAc shell, which was followed by a more modest and sustained increase lasting for the duration of the fiber photometry recordings (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with the PKA inhibitor H89 blocked the effect of DCZ to increase dopamine transient frequency.
claims.source: Pretreatment with the PKA inhibitor H89 (1 mg/kg, i.p.) blocked the effect of DCZ to increase dopamine transient frequency (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: DCZ increased the number of active nose pokes in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice under an FR1 schedule.
claims.source: DCZ increased the number of active nose pokes (Figure 6E) and cocaine infusions (Figure 6F) in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: DCZ increased the number of cocaine infusions in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice under an FR1 schedule.
claims.source: DCZ increased the number of active nose pokes (Figure 6E) and cocaine infusions (Figure 6F) in rM3D(Gs)-expressing Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: DCZ did not significantly affect active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes, or cocaine infusions in mCherry-expressing Epac2-cKO mice.
claims.source: In contrast, DCZ did not significantly affect active nose pokes, inactive nose pokes (Figure 6E), or cocaine infusions (Figure 6F) in mCherry-expressing Epac2-cKO mice, indicating that the effects of DCZ are mediated by rM3D(Gs) activation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6E-F.

claims.claim: DCZ produced an upward shift of the ascending limb of the inverted U-shaped curve of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed rM3D(Gs) in VTA dopamine neurons.
claims.source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced an upward shift of the ascending limb of the inverted U-shaped curve of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed rM3D(Gs) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed control vector (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: DCZ did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed control vector.
claims.source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced an upward shift of the ascending limb of the inverted U-shaped curve of cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed rM3D(Gs) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in Epac2-cKO mice that expressed control vector (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: hM4D(Gi) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA.
claims.source: hM4D(Gi) and mCherry were expressed in the majority of TH+ dopamine neurons (83.8 ± 4.1% and 84.7 ± 3.4%, respectively) but were not expressed in TH- neurons in the VTA (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: DCZ significantly decreased dopamine transient frequency in the NAc shell of mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) but not mCherry.
claims.source: Subcutaneous injection of DCZ (100 µg/kg) significantly decreased dopamine transient frequency in the NAc shell of mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) but not mCherry (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: DCZ significantly decreased active nose pokes in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice.
claims.source: DCZ significantly decreased the number of active nose pokes and cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice, but did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice (Figure 7D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: DCZ significantly decreased cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice.
claims.source: DCZ significantly decreased the number of active nose pokes and cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice, but did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice (Figure 7D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: DCZ did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice.
claims.source: DCZ significantly decreased the number of active nose pokes and cocaine infusions in hM4D(Gi)-expressing WT mice, but did not significantly affect active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, or inactive nose pokes in mCherry-expressing WT mice (Figure 7D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7D-E.

claims.claim: DCZ produced a downward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) in VTA dopamine neurons.
claims.source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced a downward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed mCherry (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: DCZ did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed mCherry.
claims.source: In a multiple-dose cocaine self-administration paradigm, DCZ produced a downward shift of the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed hM4D(Gi) in VTA dopamine neurons but did not alter the cocaine dose-response curve in WT mice that expressed mCherry (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Epac2-mediated enhancement of dopamine release may represent a novel and powerful mechanism that contributes to cocaine reinforcement.
claims.source: Epac2-mediated enhancement of dopamine release may therefore represent a novel and powerful mechanism that contributes to cocaine reinforcement.
claims.evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Epac2 in the mesolimbic dopamine system promotes cocaine reinforcement via enhancement of dopamine release.
claims.source: Here, we report that Epac2 in the mesolimbic dopamine system promotes cocaine reinforcement via enhancement of dopamine release.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claims.claim: The cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling pathway has been extensively studied in the context of drug addiction.
claims.source: The cAMP-PKA-CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein) signaling pathway has been extensively studied in the context of drug addiction (Nestler, 2001; Self, 2004; Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Nestler, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claims.claim: Few studies have addressed how Epac regulates the cellular and behavioral effects of drugs of abuse.
claims.source: However, few studies have addressed how the 'other' cAMP effector, Epac, regulates the cellular and behavioral effects of drugs of abuse.
claims.evidence: This claim establishes the novelty and rationale for the current study.

claims.claim: Drug self-administration provides a measure of the reinforcing efficacy of drugs of abuse and an animal's motivation to acquire rewarding drugs.
claims.source: Drug self-administration provides a measure of the reinforcing efficacy of drugs of abuse and an animal's motivation to acquire rewarding drugs (O'Connor et al., 2011; Hiranita, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Connor et al., 2011; Hiranita, 2015.

claims.claim: Cocaine and sucrose increase dopamine levels by reducing its uptake and increasing its release, respectively.
claims.source: Cocaine and sucrose increase dopamine levels by reducing its uptake and increasing its release, respectively (Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Patriarchi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson and Pierce, 2005; Patriarchi et al., 2018.

results.result: Pharmacological inhibition of Epac2 with ESI-05 dose-dependently reduced cocaine self-administration in mice under both FR1 and PR reinforcement schedules, and across a broad range of cocaine doses. ESI-05 decreased active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, and breakpoint without affecting inactive nose pokes, and produced a downward shift in the cocaine dose-response curve.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C19-C21, C23-C25 collectively demonstrate that ESI-05 reduces cocaine self-administration across multiple behavioral paradigms with appropriate statistical support (Figures 1B-H). The lack of effect on inactive nose pokes (C21) strengthens the interpretation that effects are specific to cocaine-seeking behavior rather than general motor impairment. The dose-response data (C23) and PR schedule results (C24-C25) provide converging evidence for reduced motivation to obtain cocaine.

results.result: Epac2-cKO mice were generated and validated, showing selective deletion of Epac2 from VTA dopamine neurons while maintaining normal baseline physiology. Epac2 was expressed in both dopamine and GABA neurons in WT mice but only in GABA neurons in Epac2-cKO mice, with no differences in body weight, locomotor activity, or basic electrophysiological properties of dopamine neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 provide comprehensive validation of the Epac2-cKO model through multiple complementary approaches including scRT-PCR (C27-C29), behavioral assessments (C26), and electrophysiology (C30). The selective deletion is well-documented and the lack of baseline phenotypic differences strengthens subsequent behavioral interpretations.

results.result: Epac2-cKO mice showed reduced cocaine self-administration under FR1 and PR schedules despite similar acquisition rates as WT mice. Epac2-cKO mice exhibited decreased active nose pokes, cocaine infusions, and breakpoint, with a downward shift in the cocaine dose-response curve, while inactive nose pokes remained unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C39 demonstrate that genetic deletion of Epac2 from dopamine neurons impairs cocaine self-administration across multiple behavioral measures (Figures 2A-G). The similar acquisition rates (C31-C32) but reduced maintenance (C33-C39) suggest Epac2 is not required for initial learning but is critical for ongoing cocaine reinforcement. Statistical support is provided throughout.

results.result: Neither ESI-05 treatment nor Epac2-cKO affected sucrose self-administration under FR1 or PR reinforcement schedules, indicating specificity of Epac2's role in cocaine versus natural reward reinforcement.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 provide important negative control data showing that Epac2 manipulations do not affect sucrose self-administration (Figure 3 and supplements). This specificity strengthens the interpretation that effects on cocaine self-administration are not due to general motivational or motor deficits, though the mechanistic basis for this selectivity remains unclear.

results.result: Epac2-cKO mice exhibited significantly decreased evoked dopamine release across all striatal subregions (NAc core, NAc shell, DMS, DLS) in response to both single pulse and high-frequency burst stimulation, without altering dopamine reuptake kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 demonstrate that Epac2 deletion reduces dopamine release amplitude without affecting reuptake (Figure 4). The consistent effects across multiple striatal regions and stimulation patterns strengthen the conclusion. The lack of change in decay constant τ (C46) indicates the effect is specific to release rather than clearance mechanisms.

results.result: Pharmacological activation of Epac2 with S-220 dose-dependently increased evoked dopamine release in WT slices, an effect blocked by Epac2-cKO and ESI-05 but not by PKA inhibition. Similarly, PKA activation with 6-Bnz-cAMP increased dopamine release independently of Epac2, demonstrating that Epac2 and PKA pathways independently regulate dopamine release.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 and C108 provide strong pharmacological evidence that Epac2 and PKA independently enhance dopamine release (Figure 5). The use of selective agonists and antagonists, combined with genetic deletion, provides multiple lines of converging evidence. The concentration-dependent effects (C47) and appropriate controls strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Chemogenetic stimulation of VTA dopamine neurons via rM3D(Gs) activation increased dopamine release in a PKA-dependent manner and rescued the impairment in cocaine self-administration in Epac2-cKO mice, producing an upward shift in the ascending limb of the cocaine dose-response curve.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 and C115 demonstrate that enhancing dopamine release through an Epac2-independent mechanism (Gs-DREADD) rescues the behavioral deficit in Epac2-cKO mice (Figure 6). The fiber photometry data (C55-C56) confirms increased dopamine release, and the behavioral rescue (C57-C61) supports the hypothesis that reduced dopamine release underlies the self-administration deficit. Appropriate mCherry controls strengthen the interpretation.

results.result: Chemogenetic inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons via hM4D(Gi) activation decreased dopamine release and reduced cocaine self-administration in WT mice, producing a downward shift in the cocaine dose-response curve, thereby phenocopying the effects of Epac2 disruption.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 and C116 show that inhibiting dopamine release in WT mice mimics the Epac2-cKO phenotype (Figure 7). The fiber photometry data (C63) confirms reduced dopamine release, and the behavioral effects (C64-C68) parallel those seen with Epac2 deletion. This bidirectional manipulation strengthens the causal link between dopamine release and cocaine self-administration.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background that repeated drug exposure upregulates cAMP signaling in the mesolimbic dopamine system, and that Epac2 is a major cAMP effector abundantly expressed in the brain, while the cAMP-PKA-CREB pathway has been extensively studied in addiction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C13, and C71 provide well-established background information supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the rationale for investigating Epac2's role in cocaine reinforcement and position the current work within the existing literature on cAMP signaling in addiction.

results.result: Prior work from the authors and others established that Epac2 regulates synaptic plasticity in VTA dopamine neurons, that Epac activators enhance neurotransmitter release through interactions with active zone proteins, and that RIM is required for dopamine release, providing mechanistic context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17, C72-C73 cite relevant prior work that provides mechanistic context for the current findings. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work, establishing the foundation for investigating Epac2's role in dopamine release and cocaine reinforcement.

results.result: Methodological details of cocaine self-administration training are provided, including acquisition rates, temporal patterns of responding, and dose-response characteristics in the multiple-dose paradigm.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C22, C97-C100 provide important methodological details and baseline characterization of the self-administration paradigm. The lack of sex differences (C22) justifies pooling data, and the temporal pattern analysis (C98-C99) provides additional behavioral characterization supporting the main findings.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within the broader literature on dopamine's role in reward, differential effects on drug versus natural rewards, mechanisms of dopamine release regulation, and prior DREADD studies manipulating dopamine neuron activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C84 provide appropriate contextualization of the findings through citations to relevant literature. These claims support the interpretation of results and acknowledge both consistencies and apparent discrepancies with prior work, particularly regarding differential effects on cocaine versus sucrose self-administration.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that Epac2 likely acts through multiple mechanisms beyond dopamine release facilitation, including structural plasticity, synaptic transmission regulation, and both cAMP-dependent and -independent signaling pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C95 and C124 appropriately acknowledge the complexity of Epac2 signaling and the limitations of focusing solely on dopamine release. These speculative but well-supported claims (C95, C124) recognize that the current findings do not exclude additional mechanisms and suggest directions for future research.

results.result: The authors conclude that Epac2 in the mesolimbic dopamine system promotes cocaine reinforcement via enhancement of dopamine release, representing a novel mechanism contributing to cocaine's reinforcing effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 and C121-C123 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the convergent evidence from pharmacological inhibition, genetic deletion, ex vivo dopamine release measurements, and bidirectional DREADD manipulations. The mechanistic interpretation (C121-C123) is reasonable given the data, though some aspects remain inferential.

results.result: Methodological claims regarding the Instech catheter system, FSCV measurements, pharmacological tools, viral expression patterns, DREADD actuators, fiber photometry sensors, and anatomical organization are provided.
results.evaluation: Claims C96, C104-C111, C117-C120 provide important methodological details and validation supported by appropriate citations and experimental data. The validation of GRABDA2m sensors with haloperidol (C119) and characterization of viral expression patterns (C109) strengthen confidence in the technical approaches.

results.result: Temporal pattern analysis and interpretation of dose-response curve shifts provide additional behavioral characterization, with WT mice showing regular cocaine intake patterns while Epac2-cKO mice showed sporadic intake, and interpretations of ascending limb shifts in terms of reinforcing efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 and C112-C114 provide valuable additional behavioral characterization and interpretation. The temporal pattern analysis (C101-C103) adds depth to the understanding of how Epac2 disruption affects cocaine-taking behavior. The interpretations of dose-response shifts (C112-C114) are reasonable and supported by appropriate citations, though some aspects remain speculative (C114).
